name: Tiaopijin (跳皮筋)
blurb: Chinese jump rope: a stretched elastic, chanted rhymes and a height that keeps rising
title: What Is Tiaopijin (跳皮筋)? Chinese Jump Rope, Rules and Rhymes
description: Tiaopijin (跳皮筋) is the Chinese elastic-band skipping game: two hold a long elastic, a third jumps patterns to a rhyme as it rises. Huge in the 1960s–1990s.
answer: Tiaopijin (跳皮筋, jumping the elastic) is the Chinese version of the game known in English as Chinese jump rope or elastics. Two players stretch a three-to-four-metre elastic between their legs; a third jumps a set pattern of hooks, steps and twists to the beat of a chanted rhyme, and each clean round raises the elastic, from the ankles up past the head. It was hugely popular in Chinese schoolyards from the 1960s to the 1990s, mostly among girls, and has faded since 2000. No one knows exactly where it began.

body: Two holders stand three or four metres apart with the elastic around their ankles; the jumper works in the middle. With more children, one team holds while the other jumps, swapping when every jumper on a team has made a mistake.

The jumper must complete an agreed routine built from a dozen or so basic moves: hooking the elastic with a foot, stepping over, touching, kicking, tripping, wrapping, crossing, stepping on it, turning. Missing a step, letting the elastic slip off or losing the rhythm of the rhyme ends the turn.
After each successful round the elastic moves up a level. The order varies by place, but typically runs:

ol: Top of the thighs, then waist
Ears, then the top of the head
A hand's span above the head, and finally the holders' arms raised as high as they go

body: Once the elastic is above the waist, jumpers kick a leg high to hook it down before jumping, which is where tall, flexible kids shone.

The game is almost always played to a chant whose beat sets each step. The best known begins with a ball, bananas and pears, then counts: malan kaihua ershiyi (the malan flower blooms, twenty-one), followed by numbers up to thirty-one. Other rhymes include I Am Going to School and verses about national heroes, with wording differing by region.

body.note: A popular online story says the malan line was written to mark China's first atomic bomb test in 1964, Malan being the test base. Others point to similar counting rhymes recorded in the 1950s or earlier. Its origin is disputed.

body: Needing nothing but an elastic, it filled break times for decades. From the 2000s, less free time and more screen entertainment pushed it aside. The game is international: elastics in Britain and Australia, Gummitwist in Germany, gomutobi in Japan.

faq.q: How many people do you need?
faq.a: At least three: two to hold the elastic and one to jump. Bigger groups split into a holding team and a jumping team.

faq.q: Is Chinese jump rope really from China?
faq.a: Not provably. The English name links it to China, but the game is played worldwide and its origin is undocumented.

faq.q: What was the elastic made of?
faq.a: Usually a three-to-four-metre length of rubber elastic; some children linked lots of small rubber bands into a chain.
